messages.subject: Counting the number of times a phrase occurs.
parts:
Hello,

Hopefully this is a simple question. I want to identify the number of times a particular phrase (e.g carbon tax) occurs.

In this spredsheet the following code produces the rows in which the phrase occurs but not the number of times it occurs in a row.

test <- read.csv("D:/Bolt/Bolt_part1.csv",header=T, as.is=TRUE)
z <- apply(test, 1, paste, collapse=' ')
b <- grep("carbon.tax", z)  # which rows have the match
b
 [1]  3  8 15 29 36 46 49 54 58 63 65 66 68 73 77 83 84 85 86 87 90

 gregexpr matches the number of times phrase occurs per record, for example:

[[54]]
[1] 1377 1934 2082 2710 4184
attr(,"match.length")
[1] 11 11 11 11 11

Rather than obtaining all the records such as:

[[53]]
[1] -1
attr(,"match.length")
[1] -1

How can I obtain the output for just the records with a positive match? I suspect the answer is on page 75-77 but I couldn't work out what is required.

Any assistance is appreciated.

Bob

messages.author: 97ce067823027f53
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Counting the number of times a phrase occurs.
parts:
Is this what you want? You have the matches already from the gregexpr, it’s just a matter of counting them up. 

x <- c("i love the carbon tax.", 
       "carbon tax, carbon tax.", 
       "idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.", 
       "nothing to see here.")
corpus <- data.frame(sentences=x)
corpus
res <- gregexpr("carbon tax", x)
res
mylength <- function(vec) { 
  length(vec[vec != -1])   # gregexpr returns -1 when no match, so ignore this
}
corpus$num_matches <- sapply(res, mylength)
corpus

Alex

messages.author: 8dafe35eb614235f
messages.subject: Re: Counting the number of times a phrase occurs.
parts: It wasn't clear to me whether you wanted a vector with the number of matches in each element, a single number with the total number of matches, or a new column within the data frame with the number of matches in each row. Here's how I might have approached each one, using packages not featured in QCLWR. The packages load the magrittr package, which enables the use of the forward pipe operator %>%, which can take some time to get accustomed to, but increases the (sequential) readability of the code (as opposed to an inside-out way of writing several functions).

x <- c("i love the carbon tax.", 
       "carbon tax, carbon tax.",
"idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.",
"nothing to see here.")

corpus <- data.frame(sentences=x)

# loads sweet packages
library("stringr")
library("dplyr")

# returns vector with number of matches in each element
str_extract_all(corpus$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length)

# returns single number with total matches
str_extract_all(corpus$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length) %>% sum()

# creates new column in data frame with number of matches in each record
corpus <- corpus %>% mutate(num_matches = str_extract_all(.$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length))

messages.author: 8dafe35eb614235f
messages.subject: Re: Counting the number of times a phrase occurs.
parts:
Bob, try this reproducible example (that is, an example that you can copy and paste directly into R), after you've installed "stringr" and "dplyr":

### START REPRODUCIBLE EXAMPLE ###

# creates toy data frame
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,
  sentence = c("i love the carbon tax.", "carbon tax, carbon tax.", "idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.", "nothing to see here.")
)

# loads sweet packages
library("stringr")
library("dplyr")

# summarizes number of matches by id
df %>% group_by(id) %>% summarise(num_matches = str_count(sentence, "carbon tax"))

### END EXAMPLE ###

Obviously, you'll need to change "id" in "group_by(id)" to the exact name of the variable with the id in your data frame, and "sentence" in "str_count(sentence, "carbon tax")" to the exact name of the variable with the sentences. Note that those variable names should not have spaces in them.

messages.subject: Re: Counting the number of times a phrase occurs.
parts: You can combine the several columns of text into one and then search on that one, combined column:

### START REPRODUCIBLE EXAMPLE ###

# creates toy data frame
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,

first_column = c("i love the carbon tax.", "carbon tax, carbon tax.", "idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.", "nothing to see here."),
  second_column = c("some sentence", "another one", "I hate carbon tax", "I love carbon tax. Carbon tax is the best!"),
  third_column = c("CARBON TAX IS COOL", "Whatever?!", "Carbon tax is for the birds. Carbon tax is the worse.", "You're wrong.")

)

# loads sweet packages
library("stringr")
library("dplyr")

# summarizes number of matches by id
df %>%

mutate(combined_column = paste(first_column, second_column, third_column)) %>%  # combines several columns into one new column
  group_by(id) %>%  # groups by id, so that the totals are given by id
  summarise(num_matches = str_count(combined_column, regex("carbon tax", ignore_case = T)))  # searches on the combined column; also wraps the search term "carbon tax" in regex(..., ignore_case = T) in order to find both lower-case and upper-case matches

### END EXAMPLE ###

When you get some time, read up on stringr, probably starting here:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/stringr/vignettes/stringr.html

as well as on dplyr, starting here:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/introduction.html

parts:
It may be returning what the makers of dplyr call a "local data frame", which is a wrapper around data.frame that has several characteristics, one of which is that only the first ten rows (or a few more, if the total number of rows is just above ten) print at the console:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/data_frames.html

One way to verify that the number of rows is correct is to simply call nrow() on the resulting data frame (obviously, you'll need to save the resulting data frame to a new variable or save it to the name of the original data frame).

About trying to save num_matches: 
It's not clear to me whether you want to save it to your hard drive or to move it to a vector that you can then work with more within R. QCLWR has examples of both.
